questions.stem: The north pole of one bar magnet is brought close to the north pole of another bar magnet. What happens?
options: They attract, pulling each other together
Nothing, because the two poles cancel out
They attract, but only once they touch
They repel, pushing each other apart
questions.explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract, so two north poles push each other apart. The idea that any two magnets always attract is common because a magnet sticks to so many things, but that only applies to unlike poles or to unmagnetised iron and steel.

questions.stem: Which of these metals is attracted to a magnet?
options: Copper
Aluminium
Silver
Nickel
questions.explanation: Iron, nickel and cobalt, and alloys such as steel that contain them, are magnetic materials. Copper, aluminium and silver are metals, but a magnet does not attract them — being a metal is not enough.

questions.stem: A recycling centre uses a large magnet to pull steel cans out of a mixture of steel and aluminium cans. Why does this work?
options: Aluminium cans are lighter, so the magnet cannot lift them
Aluminium cans are painted with a coating that blocks magnetism
Steel cans carry a static charge that the magnet attracts
Steel contains iron, which is magnetic, but aluminium is not
questions.explanation: Steel is mostly iron, a magnetic material, while aluminium is not magnetic at all. Lightness is not the reason: a magnet will not lift even a tiny scrap of aluminium foil. Magnets act on magnetic materials, not on electric charges.

questions.stem: Outside a bar magnet, in which direction do the magnetic field lines point?
options: From the middle out towards both poles
In loops around the middle, missing the poles
From the north pole to the south pole
From the south pole to the north pole
questions.explanation: By convention, field lines leave the north pole and curve around to enter the south pole. The direction is defined as the way the north end of a small compass would point at that spot, which is away from the magnet's north pole.

questions.stem: On a field-line diagram of a bar magnet, where is the field strongest, and how does the diagram show it?
options: At the poles, where the lines are closest together
In the middle, where the lines are the longest and straightest
At the poles, where the lines are furthest apart
Evenly all around, because the lines never cross
questions.explanation: The closer together field lines are drawn, the stronger the field, and they crowd together at the poles. That is why paperclips cling to the ends of a bar magnet rather than its middle. Long lines in the middle do not mean a strong field — line length tells you nothing about strength.

questions.stem: Iron filings are sprinkled on paper over a bar magnet and tapped gently. Why do they form a pattern of curved lines?
options: Each filing becomes a tiny magnet and lines up along the field
The filings are charged by friction and pushed by static
Gravity pulls the filings into the lowest parts of the paper
The magnet warms the paper and the filings slide off the warm parts
questions.explanation: The magnet's field magnetises each filing, and each tiny magnet turns to line up with the field at that point, tracing out the field lines. Static charge is not involved: the same pattern forms in damp air, where any charge would leak away.

questions.stem: A small plotting compass is placed near a bar magnet. Which way does the north end of the compass needle point?
options: Directly towards the magnet's north pole, wherever it sits
To geographic north, as if the magnet were not there
Across the field line, at right angles to it
Along the field line, towards the magnet's south pole
questions.explanation: The needle is itself a small magnet, so its north end is attracted to the bar magnet's south pole and lines up along the field. Pointing at the magnet's north pole would mean like poles attracting. Close to a strong magnet, the magnet's field is far stronger than Earth's, so the needle ignores geographic north.

questions.stem: The north end of a compass needle points towards Earth's geographic North Pole. What does this tell you about the magnetic pole there?
options: It is where gravity is strongest, so the needle tips that way
It is a magnetic south pole, because unlike poles attract
It is a magnetic north pole, because like poles attract
It has no magnetism; the needle lines up with Earth's spin
questions.explanation: The needle's north end is attracted there, and only unlike poles attract, so the magnetic pole near the geographic North Pole must be a south pole. Calling it a north pole mixes up the geographic name with the magnetic type. A compass lines up with Earth's magnetic field, not with its rotation or gravity.

questions.stem: A soft iron nail and a steel needle are both magnetised and then the magnet is taken away. What happens?
options: The nail loses most of its magnetism, but the needle keeps it
The needle loses its magnetism, but the nail keeps it for good
Neither can be magnetised, because both are made of metal
Both keep their magnetism forever, because both contain iron
questions.explanation: Soft iron is easy to magnetise but loses its magnetism quickly, so it makes temporary magnets — ideal for electromagnet cores. Steel is harder to magnetise but holds on to its magnetism, so it is used for permanent magnets. Both contain iron, but they behave differently once the magnet is removed.

questions.stem: What is an electromagnet?
options: A battery that stores its energy in a magnetic metal
A coil of wire that becomes magnetic when a current flows in it
A permanent magnet that produces its own electric current as it spins
A piece of iron charged by rubbing it with a cloth
questions.explanation: A current flowing through a wire produces a magnetic field, and winding the wire into a coil concentrates that field. Unlike a permanent magnet, an electromagnet only works while the current is flowing. Rubbing gives an object static charge, which is not magnetism.

questions.stem: Which change would make an electromagnet stronger?
options: Adding more turns of wire to the coil
Taking the iron core out of the coil
Lowering the current through the coil
Swapping the iron core for a copper one
questions.explanation: An electromagnet gets stronger with more turns, more current and an iron core inside the coil. Removing the core or swapping it for copper weakens it, because copper is not a magnetic material and cannot add to the field the way iron does.

questions.stem: Why do scrapyard cranes use electromagnets rather than permanent magnets?
options: They attract every kind of metal, including aluminium and copper scrap
They keep working without any electricity once the load is lifted
They contain no iron, so the crane has less weight to carry
Switching off the current drops the load exactly where it is wanted
questions.explanation: An electromagnet can be switched on to pick up steel scrap and switched off to release it, which a permanent magnet cannot do. It still only attracts magnetic materials, so aluminium and copper are not lifted. It also needs a current the whole time it holds the load.

questions.stem: Which of these depends on electromagnets to work?
options: A solar-powered calculator
A glass magnifying lens
A liquid-in-glass thermometer
A maglev train
questions.explanation: Maglev trains use powerful electromagnets to lift the train above the track and push it along. Electromagnets are also found in speakers, relays, MRI scanners and scrapyard cranes. A calculator, a lens and a thermometer work by light or heat, not magnetism.

questions.stem: A student tests whether the number of turns affects the strength of an electromagnet by counting the paperclips it picks up. What must stay the same in every trial?
options: The number of paperclips that are picked up
Nothing needs to stay the same if each trial is repeated
The current, the core and the type of paperclip
The number of turns of wire on the coil
questions.explanation: In a fair test only the independent variable — here the number of turns — is changed, and everything else that could affect the result is controlled. The number of turns cannot be kept the same because it is the thing being tested, and the paperclip count is the result being measured. Repeating trials improves reliability but does not make an uncontrolled test fair.

questions.stem: When a balloon is rubbed on a woollen jumper, which particles move from one material to the other?
options: Electrons
Protons
Neutrons
Whole atoms
questions.explanation: Rubbing transfers electrons, which sit on the outside of atoms and can be pulled off. Protons are held in the nucleus and do not move during charging by friction, so an object becomes positive by losing electrons, never by gaining protons.

questions.stem: A balloon becomes negatively charged after being rubbed on wool. What happened?
options: It lost electrons to the wool
It gained electrons from the wool
It gained positive protons from the wool
It lost protons to the wool
questions.explanation: Electrons carry negative charge, so gaining extra electrons gives the balloon an overall negative charge, and the wool, having lost them, is left positive. Protons stay locked in the nucleus during rubbing, so options involving protons moving describe something that does not happen.

questions.stem: Two balloons are both rubbed on the same woollen jumper and then hung on threads close to each other. What happens?
options: Nothing, because balloons are electrical insulators
They push apart, because they have the same charge
They pull together, because they have opposite charges
They pull together, because all charged objects attract
questions.explanation: Rubbed on the same material, both balloons pick up the same kind of charge, and like charges repel. Charged objects do not always attract — only opposite charges do. Being insulators is what lets the balloons hold their charge in the first place.

questions.stem: A negatively charged balloon sticks to a wall that has no overall charge. What explains this?
options: It repels electrons in the wall's surface, leaving the nearby surface positive
It hands its extra electrons to the wall, so the wall becomes negative
Walls are always positively charged, so they attract the balloon
Air pressure presses the light balloon flat against the wall
questions.explanation: The balloon's negative charge pushes electrons in the wall slightly away, so the surface right next to it becomes positive, and that nearby positive charge attracts the balloon. This is called induction or polarisation. If the balloon really gave its electrons to the wall, both would be negative and they would repel.

questions.stem: A charged rod touches the metal cap of an electroscope and its two thin leaves spread apart. Why?
options: Both leaves gain the same charge and repel each other
The leaves gain opposite charges and push apart
The rod warms the leaves so that they expand
The leaves become magnetised by the rod and repel each other
questions.explanation: Charge spreads through the metal cap and rod down to both leaves, giving them the same type of charge, so they repel and diverge. Opposite charges would attract, pulling the leaves together rather than apart. The effect is electrostatic, not magnetic or thermal.

questions.stem: Why can a plastic ruler be charged by rubbing, but a metal spoon held in your hand cannot?
options: Charge flows away through the metal and your body, but stays put on plastic
Metal atoms have no electrons that can be rubbed off them
Plastic contains more protons than metal, so it holds more charge
Metals can only gain positive charge, which never builds up
questions.explanation: Plastic is an insulator, so charge stays where it was rubbed on. Metal is a conductor, and any charge flows straight through it and your body to the ground. Metals certainly have electrons — the free electrons are exactly what let charge flow away.

questions.stem: What does it mean to earth a charged object?
options: To connect it to the ground so its charge can flow away
To bury it so its charge is stored safely
To rub it until it gains more charge
To turn it so that it lines up with Earth's magnetic field
questions.explanation: Earthing gives charge a conducting path to the ground, which is so large that it can take or supply electrons until the object is neutral. Lining up with Earth's magnetic field is what a compass does — that is magnetism, not static charge.

questions.stem: What causes lightning?
options: Sunlight focused by raindrops heating a narrow path through the air
Earth's magnetic field releasing its stored energy into a cloud
Hot air rising so quickly inside a cloud that it begins to glow
Charge that has built up in a storm cloud discharging through the air
questions.explanation: Inside a storm cloud, colliding ice particles separate charge, and when enough builds up it discharges as a giant spark to another cloud or the ground. A lightning bolt is the same process as the small spark you feel touching a door handle, on a far bigger scale.

questions.stem: Which list contains only non-contact forces?
options: Gravity, friction and magnetic force
Electrostatic force, air resistance and gravity
Magnetic force, tension and electrostatic force
Gravity, magnetic force and electrostatic force
questions.explanation: Gravity, magnetism and the electrostatic force all act across a gap without the objects touching. Friction, air resistance and tension need surfaces or materials in contact, so any list containing one of them includes a contact force.

questions.stem: Before a fuel tanker unloads petrol at a service station, the driver connects an earthing cable to it. Why?
options: To keep the fuel cool by conducting its heat into the ground
To protect the parked tanker from being struck by lightning
To measure how much fuel flows out of the tanker's tank
To stop static charge building up and making a spark near fuel vapour
questions.explanation: Fuel flowing through hoses can build up static charge by friction, and a spark near petrol vapour could ignite it. The earthing cable lets any charge flow safely to the ground as it forms. It has nothing to do with lightning, which is a hazard whether or not fuel is being unloaded.

questions.stem: A positively charged balloon is held near a thin stream of water from a tap, and the stream bends towards it. What explains this?
options: The balloon passes electrons to the water through the air
The balloon's magnetic field pulls on the moving water
Charges in the water shift so its near side is negative and is attracted
The water is already negatively charged, so it is drawn to the balloon
questions.explanation: The positive balloon pulls negative charge in the water slightly towards it, so the near side becomes negative and is attracted, just as a neutral wall attracts a charged balloon. Tap water has no overall charge — a negatively charged balloon bends the stream towards it too, which shows the water is not simply negative.
